query: We aim to synthesize an equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy via ink-extrusion additive manufacturing using a precursor blend of metallic and hydride powders. The process relies on the sequential thermal decomposition of hydrides (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) to drive alloying, where decomposition temperatures correlate with hydride formation enthalpies. To prevent the formation of alpha-HCP phases induced by dissolved oxygen (an alpha-stabilizer) which would otherwise degrade mechanical properties, the sintering atmosphere must be strictly controlled using an oxygen getter. The goal is to achieve a nearly fully dense microstructure where slow cooling results in a dual-phase (alpha-BCC + beta-BCC) structure, but a rapid quench from the homogenization temperature traps a metastable single-phase beta-BCC structure. Propose a hypothesis for the specific oxygen getter material and sintering regime that balances dehydrogenation kinetics with oxygen scavenging, predict the resulting phase constitution and grain size after rapid quenching, and design a falsification experiment using in-situ X-ray diffraction to verify the sequence of phase transformations and the absence of alpha-Ti during the critical decomposition window.

generation.hypothesis: Using TiH2 as an in-situ oxygen getter during sequential hydride decomposition in ink-extrusion additive manufacturing of equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will scavenge oxygen below the critical threshold for alpha-Ti precipitation, enabling a fully dense, single-phase beta-BCC microstructure after rapid quenching from the homogenization temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic blend of metallic Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, Zr powders and hydrides (TaH0.5, NbH, HfH2, TiH2, ZrH2) with initial oxygen content <0.5 wt%
generation.intervention: Ink-extrusion additive manufacturing followed by sequential thermal decomposition of hydrides (TaH0.5: ~400°C, NbH: ~500°C, HfH2: ~600°C, TiH2: ~700°C, ZrH2: ~800°C) with TiH2 acting as an in-situ oxygen getter, followed by homogenization at 1200°C and rapid water quenching
generation.conditions: Atmosphere: High-purity argon with TiH2-derived oxygen scavenging; Heating rate: 10°C/min; Homogenization: 1200°C for 2h; Cooling: Water quenching (<100°C/s)
generation.structural_mediator: TiH2 decomposition releases Ti and H2, with Ti reacting with oxygen to form TiO2 (stable oxide) before alpha-Ti can precipitate, maintaining oxygen in solid solution below 0.8 wt% threshold
generation.mechanism: Sequential hydride decomposition drives alloying while TiH2 acts as a sacrificial oxygen getter; TiO2 formation prevents alpha-Ti precipitation by sequestering oxygen; rapid quenching suppresses alpha-BCC nucleation, trapping metastable beta-BCC phase
generation.predicted_outcome: Fully dense (>98% theoretical density) single-phase beta-BCC microstructure with grain size 1-5 μm, oxygen content <0.8 wt%, no alpha-Ti or HfO2 precipitates, Vickers hardness ~350 HV10
generation.baseline: Conventional sintering without oxygen getter results in alpha-BCC + beta-BCC dual-phase structure with 1.07 wt% oxygen, HfO2 precipitates, and grain size ~4 μm with porosity
generation.boundary: Valid for oxygen content <1.0 wt% in initial powders; fails if hydride decomposition temperatures overlap significantly or if cooling rate <50°C/s
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty in exact decomposition temperature overlap between hydrides; potential for incomplete oxygen scavenging if TiH2 stoichiometry is insufficient; grain size prediction assumes no grain growth during homogenization
generation.falsification_experiment: In-situ X-ray diffraction during hydride decomposition (400-900°C) to monitor: (1) absence of alpha-Ti peaks (100), (2) formation of TiO2 peaks, (3) evolution of BCC phase fraction; post-quench XRD to confirm single-phase beta-BCC; SEM/EDS to verify oxygen distribution and absence of HfO2/TiO2 precipitates; if alpha-Ti or HfO2 detected, hypothesis falsified

cited_evidence.text: The Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti alloy in the form of buttons was prepared by vacuum arc melting of the nominal mixtures of the corresponding elements. The degrees of purity of Ta, Nb, Hf, Zr, and Ti were 99.9%, 99.9%, 99.7%, 99% and 99.7%, respectively. Melting was conducted in a high-purity argon atmosphere. High-purity molten titanium was used as a getter for residual oxygen, nitrogen, and hydrogen. In order to achieve homogeneous distribution of the elements in the alloys, the buttons were turned upside down and re-melted four times. The buttons were approximately 13 mm thick and 35 mm in diameter and had a shiny surface. Following this stage, the alloys were cast into bars of 9 mm in diameter and 85 mm in length. One group of specimens was left to solidify inside the mold after casting. Namely, it underwent a process of gravity casting. The other group was cast by applying suction by means of a vacuum pump. The last stage was Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP), HIP is a common practice, involving high temperatures and isostatic pressure and it is used for closing internal porosity [ [12] ]. Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content.
